Enthusiast of the Month: Matt Brown

55 years of listening, from a Patrolman 9 and Radio Nederland QSL cards to monthly DX reports on the air.

55 yrs SWL / DXer · Pre-1990 Most active years · ~25 SWLs in his RFI listeners club · 3 Primary radios today

“My brother happened to get a radio that had shortwave capability, redefining for my young self what distant listening really was.”
— Matt Brown

Radios: Sangean 803, Panasonic RF-2200 and XHDATA D-219 are his primary radios.

Antenna: A long wire for now, with a better loop antenna planned for when he returns to more serious listening.

It started with AM radio

Matt fell in love with distant listening around age 8, tuning far-off AM stations. In the 1960s there was much less noise on the AM band, so stations from around the U.S. came in easily, and he loved the idea of hearing them.

Then came shortwave

At 11 or 12 his brother got a radio with shortwave, which redefined what distant listening meant. His dad bought him a Patrolman 9, and his very first QSL cards followed: Radio Nederland in Holland, then Radio Moscow, HCJB and more.

The night Idi Amin came on the air

His most memorable shortwave moment: Radio Uganda could be received only sporadically back then, but one evening he tuned in and listened to the dictator Idi Amin ramble on endlessly with his political diatribes against the world. Because it was Idi Amin himself, it made for a very memorable experience.

Giving back to the hobby

  • Taped monthly DX reports that were broadcast on Adventist World Radio India, Radio Clarín in Santo Domingo, and Austrian Radio
  • Headed a group of some 25 SWLs of Radio France Internationale and published a monthly “Listeners Club” bulletin for almost two years
  • Wrote a few simple articles about the hobby for the old SPEEDX shortwave listeners club’s monthly bulletin

Listening today

Matt has been a more casual listener for the last 10 to 15 years, but the dial still calls. His long wire antenna gets him by for now, and a better loop is on the list for the day he gets back to more serious listening.

What’s next

He has “so much more to write about” and has thought about writing an academic-style paper for people curious about shortwave in its golden era, the 1970s and 1980s. “We’ll see,” he says.

Did you hear Radio Uganda, or another golden-era broadcast you still remember? Share it on our Radio Memories page.
